items.prompt_md: Why does the first arrival at a node in BFS give its shortest distance on an unweighted graph?
options: The FIFO queue processes all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1
BFS always picks the cheapest edge first
The visited set sorts nodes by distance
BFS tries all routes and keeps the minimum
items.answer: The FIFO queue processes all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1
items.explanation_md: Queue order means closer nodes are always dequeued first, so the first discovery is via a fewest-edges route. Picking the cheapest edge is the idea behind Dijkstra, and BFS never compares routes.

items.prompt_md: In BFS you should mark a node as visited:
options: When you dequeue it, since that is when you process it
When you enqueue it, so it can never be queued twice
Only when you reach the goal
After the whole ring is finished
items.answer: When you enqueue it, so it can never be queued twice
items.explanation_md: Marking at enqueue stops several neighbours in the same ring from pushing the same node. Marking at dequeue still gives the right answer but lets duplicates pile up and can exceed time limits.

items.prompt_md: A BFS on a grid computes `dist` by wrapping the dequeue loop in `for _ in range(len(queue))`. What does each pass of that outer loop represent?
options: One single node being processed
One row of the grid
One complete ring: every node at the same distance from the start
One neighbour direction
items.answer: One complete ring: every node at the same distance from the start
items.explanation_md: Taking len(queue) at the start of a pass freezes the size of the current ring; nodes appended during the pass belong to the next ring. That is how queue order becomes a distance number.

items.prompt_md: Why can a plain DFS not be trusted for shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
options: DFS cannot track visited nodes
DFS only works on trees
DFS uses a queue so it explores in the wrong order
It commits to the first route it finds, which can be much longer than the best one
items.answer: It commits to the first route it finds, which can be much longer than the best one
items.explanation_md: DFS dives deep along one branch and reaches the goal by whatever route that is. Marking visited cells makes this worse because it will not re-open them to find a shorter route. It does handle visited sets and general graphs, and it uses a stack, not a queue.

items.prompt_md: For the lock puzzle (4 wheels, each turned one notch up or down per move), what is a graph node and what is an edge?
options: A node is a 4-digit combination; an edge joins combinations one wheel-turn apart
A node is a wheel; an edge is a digit
A node is a move; an edge is a combination
The graph is not defined until all edges are stored in a list
items.answer: A node is a 4-digit combination; an edge joins combinations one wheel-turn apart
items.explanation_md: Implicit graphs generate neighbours from the state on demand. Forbidden combinations are simply never expanded, which you can do by pre-loading them into the visited set.

items.prompt_md: A BFS must return -1 when the goal is unreachable. How does the loop detect this?
options: dist exceeds the number of nodes
The queue becomes empty before the goal is ever dequeued
The visited set equals the grid size
It cannot be detected without DFS
items.answer: The queue becomes empty before the goal is ever dequeued
items.explanation_md: Every reachable node is enqueued eventually. If the queue drains without hitting the goal, no route exists. The visited set equals the grid size only if all cells were reachable, which is unrelated.

items.prompt_md: What is the time complexity of BFS over a graph with V nodes and E edges, marking visited at enqueue?
options: O(V * E), since every node scans every edge
O(V log V), because the queue is sorted by distance
O(V + E): each node is enqueued and dequeued once and each edge is examined a constant number of times
O(2^V), since all routes are explored
items.answer: O(V + E): each node is enqueued and dequeued once and each edge is examined a constant number of times
items.explanation_md: The visited set guarantees each node enters the queue once, and examining its neighbours costs its degree. Summed over all nodes, that is V + E.

items.prompt_md: BFS on an n x n grid with 8-direction moves. What are the time and space costs?
options: O(n) time and O(n) space
O(n^2) time and O(1) space
O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space
O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space
items.answer: O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space
items.explanation_md: There are n^2 cells, each handled once with a constant 8 neighbour checks. The seen set and queue can hold a large part of the grid at once, so space is O(n^2) too.

items.prompt_md: A BFS searches an implicit graph where each state has b neighbours and the goal is d steps away. Roughly how many states can it enqueue before finding the goal?
options: Up to about b^d, bounded by the total number of distinct states
About b * d
About d only
About b + d
items.answer: Up to about b^d, bounded by the total number of distinct states
items.explanation_md: Each ring can be up to b times bigger than the previous one, so the frontier can grow exponentially in the distance, capped by the number of distinct states. This is why bidirectional search is a common follow-up.

items.prompt_md: Compared with a recursive DFS on a large grid, how does BFS differ in extra memory?
options: BFS uses O(1) memory while DFS uses O(n^2)
BFS holds a frontier queue (up to a ring's width) and no recursion stack, so it avoids deep-recursion overflows
BFS and DFS use exactly the same memory in every case
BFS needs no visited set
items.answer: BFS holds a frontier queue (up to a ring's width) and no recursion stack, so it avoids deep-recursion overflows
items.explanation_md: BFS needs the visited set and the queue of the current frontier, both potentially large, but no call stack. DFS recursion depth can reach the number of cells and overflow the stack.

items.prompt_md: Given a maze of open and blocked squares where each move steps to an adjacent square, find the fewest moves from the entrance to the exit.
options: DFS flood fill with a visited set
Backtracking over every route
BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
Union-find
items.answer: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
items.explanation_md: Uniform-cost moves and a minimum count mean ring-by-ring BFS. DFS flood fill finds reachability but not the fewest moves, and backtracking would enumerate every route.

items.prompt_md: A word list is given. Changing one letter at a time, each intermediate word must be in the list. Find the shortest chain of changes from one word to another.
options: Dijkstra with a priority queue
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
Topological sort
BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
items.answer: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
items.explanation_md: States are words, edges are one-letter changes, and each change counts as 1, so BFS on an implicit graph gives the shortest chain. Dijkstra is only needed when changes have different costs.

items.prompt_md: A road network has a travel time on every road. Find the quickest way from one city to another.
options: Dijkstra with a priority queue
BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
DFS flood fill with a visited set
Topological sort
items.answer: Dijkstra with a priority queue
items.explanation_md: Edges have different weights, so ring order is not distance order. Dijkstra with a priority queue is the weighted counterpart of BFS.

items.prompt_md: A puzzle board has 6 tiles and one gap, and a move slides a tile into the gap. Find the minimum number of slides to reach the solved arrangement.
options: DFS flood fill with a visited set
BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
Backtracking over every route
items.answer: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
items.explanation_md: Board arrangements are nodes, each slide is a unit-cost edge, and the minimum is wanted. BFS over the implicit state graph answers it; DFS could wander or return a long solution.

items.prompt_md: Given a grid of land and water, count the number of separate islands.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
Dijkstra with a priority queue
DFS flood fill with a visited set
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
items.answer: DFS flood fill with a visited set
items.explanation_md: No distances are asked for; each region just has to be visited once and counted. A flood fill is enough, and a distance-ring BFS adds nothing.

items.prompt_md: List every possible route through a small grid that visits each open cell at most once.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
DFS flood fill with a visited set
Union-find
Backtracking over every route
items.answer: Backtracking over every route
items.explanation_md: All routes are required, so cells must be unmarked after each route. A shortest-path BFS finds one distance, and a flood fill would only visit each cell once.

items.prompt_md: In a social network, find the smallest number of introductions needed to connect person A to person B.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
Dijkstra with a priority queue
Topological sort
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
items.answer: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
items.explanation_md: Each introduction is an edge of equal cost, and the smallest count of edges is the shortest path in an unweighted graph, which is BFS.

items.prompt_md: You may move only right or down through a grid of costs, and want the cheapest total from the top-left to the bottom-right corner.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
Dijkstra with a priority queue
Union-find
items.answer: Dynamic programming over (row, col)
items.explanation_md: Restricting moves to right and down makes the state just (row, col), so a DP table fills in order. The costs are also not uniform, so BFS rings would be wrong.

items.prompt_md: Tasks have prerequisites. Output an order in which all tasks can be completed.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
DFS flood fill with a visited set
Topological sort
Dijkstra with a priority queue
items.answer: Topological sort
items.explanation_md: The question asks for a valid ordering that respects dependencies, not a distance. Topological sort is built for that.

items.prompt_md: Cities are linked by flights with different ticket prices, but you may use at most k flights. Find the cheapest trip.
options: BFS with a queue, counting rings of distance
DFS flood fill with a visited set
Union-find
Dijkstra with a priority queue
items.answer: Dijkstra with a priority queue
items.explanation_md: Prices differ per edge, so the fewest-hops BFS does not minimise cost, and the hop limit is a bounded-hops twist handled in advanced-graphs (Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford style).
